summary: This document updates IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and its subnet variants so that a node owning or connected to a prefix can register it with neighbor routers. The registration says the prefix is reachable through the node. It updates several RFCs including RFC 4861 and RFC 8505.

plainLanguage.summary: In a low-power network, a small router usually keeps track of the addresses that devices use, so it can forward traffic to them. This document lets a device register a whole prefix, such as the range of addresses behind it, instead of single addresses. The router then treats that range as reachable through the device and can pass it on to the rest of the network.

subtitle: Letting a node register a whole prefix of addresses with its neighbor router.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Subnet Neighbor Discovery lets a constrained node register single addresses with a router, but a node that owns or fronts a whole prefix, such as a border router to a stub network, had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: The Neighbor Solicitation with an Extended Address Registration Option gets a new P-Field value of 3 and a 7-bit prefix length from 16 to 120, so the node registers a prefix and can set the R flag to ask the router to redistribute it in whatever routing protocol it runs, such as RPL.
tldr.outcome: A router can learn that a prefix is reachable through a node without a loop, keep a separate record for each registrant, and route to the registrant with the longest matching prefix, all without the node sending multicast or becoming a router itself.

today: RFC 9926 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2026. It updates RFC 4861, RFC 6550, RFC 8505, RFC 8928 and RFC 9010, and has not itself been obsoleted, so it is the current way to register a prefix with an IPv6 neighbor router.

sections.title: Why Prefix Registration in Low-Power Networks
sections.content:
The design of Low Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) is generally focused on saving energy, the most constrained resource of all. Other design constraints, such as limited memory, duty cycling of the devices and low-power lossy transmissions, follow from that concern. The radio is a major energy drain, and the LLN protocols must let the nodes sleep with the radio turned off most of the time.

Examples of LLNs include hub-and-spoke access links such as Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Low Energy, Mesh-Under networks where routing is handled at layer 2, and route-over networks such as Wi-SUN and 6TiSCH mesh networks, which use 6LoWPAN and RPL over IEEE 802.15.4.

The classical Neighbor Discovery Protocol was defined for serial links and shared transit media such as Ethernet, at a time when layer 2 broadcast was cheap on those media while memory for the neighbor cache was expensive. It was designed as a reactive protocol that relies on caching and multicast operations for Duplicate Address Detection and Address Resolution. Those multicast operations typically affect every node on the link when at most one is really targeted, which wastes energy and implies that all nodes are awake to hear the request, which conflicts with power-saving modes.

Subnet Neighbor Discovery evolved from that, following the energy conservation principles: put the protocol complexity in the less-constrained routers, use host-triggered unicast operations, and keep the use of asynchronous layer 2 broadcasts to a minimum. The Address Registration Option of RFC 6775, updated into the Extended Address Registration Option by RFC 8505, lets a registering node ask a router to inject a unicast IPv6 address in the local routing protocol and provide return reachability for that address, in a way that does not depend on which routing protocol is in use.

This document extends that mechanism to prefixes. A node that owns or is directly connected to a prefix can register that prefix with its neighbor routers, saying that the prefix can be reached through the node without a loop. The node can also ask those routers to redistribute the prefix in whatever routing protocol they run. The energy conservation principles are retained, so the node does not have to send or expect asynchronous multicast messages, and an energy-conserving node is not made into a router: it is a design choice not to use Router Advertisement messages that would make the node look like a router to its peers.
sections.plainLanguage: Low-power networks, such as sensor networks built on radio links, spend most of their energy keeping the radio off. That rules out the ordinary IPv6 neighbor discovery, which relies on broadcast messages that wake every device on the link. The alternative here uses unicast messages to a router, and this document extends it from single addresses to whole prefixes.

sections.title: How Prefix Registration Works
sections.content:
The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery operation is agnostic to the routing protocol used in the subnet. A typical route-over LLN has one or more border routers acting as the RPL Root, intermediate routers that propagate routing information towards the Root, routers that are RPL-aware, and leaf nodes that are not RPL-aware and need Neighbor Discovery to obtain reachability for their addresses and, with this document, their prefixes as well.

The operation for prefixes is the same as the operation for unicast addresses unless stated otherwise. Forwarding a packet still happens as specified in Section 11 of RFC 6550, including loop avoidance and detection, though in the case of multicast several copies may be generated.

RFC 8505 is a prerequisite: a node that implements this document MUST also implement RFC 8505. No new option is introduced. Instead, the P-Field gets a new value, 3, meaning that the registration is for a prefix rather than a single address. With that, a node can express its willingness to receive traffic for every address in a range.

Several nodes acting as border routers to the same external network, or as access routers to the same subnet, may register the same prefix with the same router or with different routers. If the R flag is set in one of the registrations for a prefix, then the router MUST redistribute the prefix in the routing protocols it takes part in, according to its redistribution policy. The duration of the redistribution is based on the longest registration lifetime across the non-expired registrations for that prefix.

The document introduces one new term. The Origin is the node that issued the prefix advertisement, either as an NS with an EARO or as a DAO with a Transit Information Option and an RPL Target Option.
sections.plainLanguage: A node that wants to be reachable tells the router about itself. This document lets it do the same for a range of addresses, so that the router can forward traffic for that whole range to the node. The router keeps one record per registering node and merges the records when it passes the information on. A router can also be asked to advertise the prefix in the routing protocol it runs.

sections.title: Advertising a Prefix in the Target Address
sections.content:
RFC 4861 expects the NS and NA exchange to be about a unicast address, which is indicated in the Target Address field of the ND message. Section 5.5 of RFC 8505 extends that to carry the Registered Address. This document updates RFC 4861 by allowing a node to advertise a prefix in the Target Address field when the message is used for a registration. In that case the prefix length MUST be indicated in the EARO of the NS message, overloading the field that the NA response uses for the Status.

If the registering node owns at least one IPv6 address derived from the registered prefix with a non-zero interface identifier, it MUST indicate one of those addresses in full in the Target Address field of the NS(EARO) message. Otherwise it MUST indicate the prefix padded with zeros.
sections.plainLanguage: The address of the registering node stays in the message in the usual place. If the node owns an address inside the prefix it registers, it puts that full address there. If it does not, it puts the prefix itself, padded with zeros.

sections.title: The P-Field Value 3 and the Registration Operation
sections.content:
RFC 9685 defines a 2-bit P-Field with values 0 through 2 and reserves the value 3 for future use. This document defines that value. When the P-Field is set to 3, the Registered Address represents a prefix rather than a single address. A receiver of an NS(EARO) message with the P-Field set to 3 MUST install a route to the indicated prefix via the source address of that message.

The registration operation itself gains behaviour. The EARO status that asks for a registration refresh now applies to prefixes as well: a router that expects to reboot can send an asynchronous NA(EARO) with that status so that peer nodes reregister all the addresses and prefixes they had registered with it. Such a message SHOULD go to the all-nodes link-scope multicast address, with the Target set to the link-local address the node previously exposed to accept registrations, the TID set to 0 and the ROVR set to all zeros. In an environment with unreliable transmissions the message may be resent in a fast sequence with the TID incremented each time, and a node that recently processed one such request ignores further requests for the duration of the fast sequence, which is 10 seconds by default.

Duplicate detection changes from address-based to prefix-overlap based. Whether overlapping addresses and prefixes may be registered is a network policy decision and is out of scope. The same prefix may be injected twice as long as both registrations use the same ROVR value. When overlapping registrations are allowed, the longest prefix match wins: routes for the registered prefixes are installed towards the node that registered with the longest prefix match, all the way to /128. Overlaps may be desirable, for instance when a router or a proxy registers a prefix or an aggregation while a host using an address from that prefix also registers its own piece.

A router that acts as a border router to external prefixes, or owns them entirely, SHOULD register all of them on every interface from which it might need to relay traffic to that prefix. It MUST set the P-Field to 3 and set the R flag to receive the traffic for those prefixes. It MAY refrain from registering a prefix on one interface if that prefix is already registered on another interface, or if it handled the EDAR and EDAC exchange itself, so that the prefix ownership is known and validated by the border router.

A node MAY set the R flag to ask the router to redistribute the prefix on other links using a routing protocol, and the router MUST NOT reregister that prefix with yet another router unless loops are avoided, for example by following a tree structure.

The router and the border router are extended to accept more than one registration for the same prefix, since several nodes may register it. The ROVR in the EARO identifies a registration uniquely within the namespace of the Registered Prefix. The router MUST maintain a registration state per tuple of IPv6 prefix, prefix length and ROVR, and SHOULD notify the border router with an EDAR message unless it has determined that the border router is legacy and does not support this specification. The border router in turn MUST maintain a registration state per tuple of IPv6 prefix and ROVR.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration option has a small field that says what is being registered: one address, a multicast address, an anycast address, and now a prefix. When it says prefix, the router installs a route to the whole range. If two registrations overlap, the more specific one wins. A router can also ask all devices on the link to register again, for instance before it restarts.

sections.title: The EARO Prefix Length Field and the F Flag
sections.content:
The EARO extends the ARO option of RFC 6775. Its Status field is used only when the EARO appears in an NA message. This document repurposes that field to carry the prefix length when the EARO appears in an NS message. The prefix length is expressed as 7 bits, with the most significant bit of the field reserved. A 7-bit value of 0 is understood as a truncated 128, meaning that the registration is for an address rather than a prefix. That keeps the option backward compatible and lets it cover both addresses and prefixes.

A new F flag signals that the Registered Prefix is topologically correct through the Registering Node. This means that the node relays packets that are sourced in the Registered Prefix to the outside, in accordance with ingress filtering for source address spoofing. The receiver then forwards packets to the Registering Node when the source address of the packet derives from the Registered Prefix. To avoid loops the receiver must be on the inside, so that packets sent by the sender towards the outside never reach it; inside and outside are administratively defined, for example a particular layer 2 network such as an Ethernet fabric as the inside.

When the F flag is not set, the Registering Node owns the prefix and delivers packets to the destination if the destination address derives from it. When the F flag is set, the node forwards traffic whose source address derives from the Registered Prefix to a network location, such as an ISP provider edge, where that source address is topologically correct.

The EDAR message gains the same P-Field value. When the P-Field is 3, the prefix is assumed to be at most 120 bits long, padded with zeros up to 120 bits, and the remaining byte carries one reserved bit and the Prefix Length. The Prefix field is a 15-byte field that carries up to 120 bits of the prefix, and the Prefix Length is a 7-bit unsigned integer with a value in the inclusive range of 16 to 120. The receiver MUST treat the padding as zeroed and MUST overwrite any unused bits with zeros before using the prefix.

Support is announced in the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option. The new bit 16, the F flag there, tells the node that the router accepts IPv6 prefix registrations, will route packets for matching addresses to the registering nodes, and will redistribute the route if the R flag is set.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries the length of the prefix in a field that used to mean something else, so old and new devices can live side by side. A new flag says that traffic from the prefix is meant to leave the network through this node, which tells the router to send such traffic back to it. The duplicate address request message gets the same treatment.

sections.title: Redistributing the Prefix in the Routing Protocol
sections.content:
With RFC 9010, a 6LoWPAN Router injects only unicast routes in RPL. When a registration carries the R flag set to 1 in the EARO, the 6LR injects the address in the RPL unicast support, and when it receives a packet directed to a unicast address for which it has an active registration it delivers the packet as a unicast layer 2 frame to the link-layer address of the node that registered the address.

This document adds the prefix case. Upon a registration with the R flag set to 1 and the P-Field set to 3, the 6LR injects the prefix in RPL using a prefix RPL Target Option, and the P-Field in that option MUST be set to 3. Upon receiving a packet directed to an address that derives from a prefix for which it has at least one registration, the 6LR delivers a copy of the packet as a unicast layer 2 frame to the link-layer address of exactly one of the nodes that registered that prefix, using the longest prefix match to find the best node.

RFC 6550 uses the Path Sequence in the Transit Information Option to retain only the freshest unicast route and drop stale ones, for example in the case of mobility. RFC 9010 copies the TID from the EARO into the Path Sequence and the ROVR into the associated Target Option, so that the registering node and the order of registration can be identified for each advertisement. This document requires that, for prefix routes, the Path Sequence is used between and only between advertisements for the same Target and from the same origin, that is, with the same ROVR value, and in that case only the freshest advertisement is retained. The freshness comparison cannot apply if the origin is not determined.

RFC 6550 uses the Path Lifetime in the Transit Information Option to say how long an advertisement stays valid, and a Path Lifetime of 0 invalidates the route. RFC 9010 maps the Address Registration lifetime in the EARO and the Path Lifetime in the Transit Information Option so they are comparable. The RPL router that merges multiple advertisements for the same prefix MUST use and advertise the longest remaining lifetime across all the origins of the advertisements for that prefix. When the lifetime expires the router sends a no-path DAO, with a lifetime of 0, using the same ROVR value as for the previous advertisements.

The proxy operation of the IPv6 Backbone Router is updated too. The proxy MUST use the P-Field as received in the EDAR or NS(EARO) message to generate the proxied NS(EARO), and it MUST use the exact same prefix and prefix length as received.
sections.plainLanguage: When the node asks for it, the router advertises the prefix in the routing protocol of the low-power network, using the same kind of route option it already uses for addresses. Traffic for any address in the prefix is then delivered to exactly one of the nodes that registered it, choosing the one whose prefix matches most precisely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document updates RFC 8505, and the security considerations of that document apply here as well. In particular the link layer SHOULD be sufficiently protected to prevent rogue access, since a rogue node with physical access to the network may inject packets and perform an attack from within.

Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery is leveraged to prevent a rogue node from registering a unicast address that it does not own. That method cannot be used with node-local autoconfigured keypairs, because they protect a single ownership only and several nodes may register the same prefix. For a prefix, as for an anycast or multicast address, it is still possible to use it to enforce the right to register: a keypair MUST be created and associated with the prefix before the prefix is deployed, and a ROVR MUST be generated from that keypair. The prefix and the ROVR MUST then be installed in the border router at the first registration, or by an external mechanism such as IP Address Management or DHCPv6 snooping prior to the first registration. The border router can then recognize the prefix on future registrations and validate the right to register based on the ROVR. The keypair MUST then be provisioned in each node that needs to register the prefix or a prefix within it, so that the node can follow the registration steps.
sections.plainLanguage: The link itself should be protected, because a rogue device with physical access can inject packets. To stop a device claiming a prefix it does not own, the border router can be given a key pair for that prefix before it is deployed, so that later registrations are checked against it.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Devices with different levels of support may coexist. A legacy node will not register prefixes, and the service is the same when the network is upgraded. A legacy router will not set the F flag in the 6CIO, and an upgraded node will not register prefixes with that router, though it may with other routers that do support this document. On an EDAR message, a legacy border router may not realize that the address being registered comes with a whole prefix and may answer that it is a duplicate, so a 6LR MUST ignore a duplicate status for prefixes.

In an RPL-based route-over LLN, a leaf registers its addresses and prefixes to a router using a layer 2 unicast NS with an EARO. The registration state is periodically renewed by the registering node before the lifetime in the EARO expires at the router. The router uses an Extended Duplicate Address Request and Confirmation exchange with the border router to notify it of the presence of the listeners. A router that owns a prefix, or provides reachability to an external prefix, but is not an RPL router can also register those prefixes with the R flag set, to give the prefix reachability inside the RPL domain.

A shared link is a case where more than one prefix is deployed over one layer 2 link and not every node is aware of every prefix. Two routers own prefixes P1 and P2 and advertise them over the same link. If one of them provides access to the outside and the other knows it as its default gateway, the second registers P2 to the first, and the first installs a route to P2 via the second, so that addresses deriving from P2 can still be reached. The second may then use ICMP Redirect messages to shorten the path between the first and the nodes that own those addresses. If P2 was delegated by the first router, the expectation is that the first aggregates P1 and P2 in its advertisements to the outside and there is no need to set the R flag, but unless the second router knows that, for instance through configuration, it SHOULD set the R flag to ask for the prefix to be advertised.

A hub link with stub spokes is the same pattern with several stub links around a backbone. Routers behind the stubs register their prefixes to the hub router, so that nodes on a stub link that derive their addresses from the stub prefix can still be reached via the hub router and then the stub router. Where two routers serve the same stub link and both register the same prefix, the hub router applies its own load-balancing logic to use either of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks will be upgraded one device at a time, and the document says what happens in the meantime: a node that meets an old router simply does not register prefixes with it. It also works through three common network shapes, a shared link, a hub with stub spokes, and a RPL network, showing how a router behind a stub link registers its prefix with the hub router so that traffic can still arrive.
